prerequisites: General knowledge of mathematics, chemistry, and physics at ASO level.
Participation certificate in a calibration test for Bachelor of Engineering Science courses.

learning_outcomes.text: The student has acquired a basic understanding of the relationships between the internal structure of a material, material properties, the history of a material, and its application in products or processes.
The student has built this understanding for various material families (polymers, metals, ceramics, and composites).

The student can apply this understanding to a number of material properties (density, stiffness, strength, fracture toughness, fatigue strength, thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity, and dielectric behavior).
The student knows the orders of magnitude of these property values.
The student can predict microstructures using binary phase diagrams and knowledge of phase transformations.
The student can perform a simple material selection.
The student can take sustainability aspects into account during material selection.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to Materials Science and its relevance in engineering education
Origin and availability of key materials
Importance of materials science for sustainable technological development
Structure of solid materials: types of atomic bonds
Ordering of atoms in crystal structures and consequences for electron configurations
Defects in different material classes, their influence and necessity
Importance of defects in controlling diffusion-controlled processes
Elastic and plastic material behavior, and fracture behavior

Quantification of structural material properties (density, stiffness modulus, torsion modulus, bulk modulus, Poisson's ratio, yield strength, tensile strength, fracture strain, fracture toughness, fatigue limit)
Mechanical behavior of materials from different material classes (metals, ceramics, polymers, composites)
Importance of dislocation movement in metals and its manipulation for strength variation
Use of phase diagrams for controlling heat treatments and manipulating mechanical properties of metals
Elastic and plastic deformation behavior of ceramic materials, emphasizing defects and diffusion
Fracture aspects of ceramics and their statistical character
Mechanical behavior of polymers based on crystallinity and molecular structure
Temperature dependence of mechanical behavior of polymers
Mechanical behavior of composite materials (particle- and fiber-reinforced, polymer, metal, and ceramic matrix)
Fracture of materials: phenomena leading to fracture under single and cyclic loading (fatigue)
Difference between brittle and ductile fracturing materials
Concepts from fracture mechanics: fracture toughness and critical defect size
Goodman and Miner's laws for predicting fatigue behavior under real cyclic loads
Paris's law for predicting crack propagation rate and total lifespan of cyclically loaded objects with defects
Binary phase diagrams: predicting phases based on pressure, temperature, and composition
Gibbs' phase rule and invariant points (eutectic, eutectoid, peritectic)
Fe-C phase diagram
Importance of phase transformations and heat treatments for modifying metallic material properties
Liquid-solid phase transitions (solidification processes)
Solid-solid phase transitions: interplay of thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic processes (diffusion)
Diffusion-controlled and diffusionless (martensitic) phase transitions
Importance of heat treatments for controlling microstructures and properties (precipitation heat treatment, recovery, and recrystallization of cold-worked metals)
Electrical properties of metallic conductors, semiconductors, and dielectrics
Relation to electron configuration and superconducting behavior in conductors
Intrinsic, p-type, and n-type extrinsic semiconductors
Piezoelectric, pyroelectric, and ferroelectric materials within dielectrics
Importance of electrical polarization curve and associated hysteresis
Fundamental thermal properties: heat capacity, thermal expansion, thermal diffusivity
Comparison of thermal properties across material classes
Heat transfer via thermal conduction by phonons and electrons; individual contributions to thermal conductivity
Thermal stresses in layered multimaterials under thermal loading
Material selection methodology (Ashby) for scientifically choosing the most suitable material for an application
Demo session: contemporary materials science research linked to basic concepts from lectures
assessment_rules: The assessment is a closed-book written exam with open questions and exercises, testing insight, basic knowledge, and synthesis ability. A formulary provided via Toledo may be brought to the exam, unmarked. A test on the demo session can yield one extra point out of 20. Students whose native language is not Dutch may use one non-technical translating dictionary, provided they report to the ombuds by specific deadlines.
